summary: In PIM Sparse Mode, a designated router sends periodic Null-Register messages to the rendezvous point to show that a multicast source is still active, one message per source and group. This document defines a way to put information about many sources and groups into a single packed PIM message, reducing message overhead.

eli5.summary: Instead of mailing one postcard per friend to say you're still here, you write one letter listing everyone. It uses fewer envelopes and less work.

questions: how to reduce pim register messages
subtitle: Bundle many PIM Null-Register and Register-Stop records into a single message to cut router chatter.

tldr.problem: In PIM Sparse Mode, the designated router sends a separate Null-Register to the rendezvous point for each active multicast source and group, so message count grows with the number of sources.
tldr.mechanism: Two new message types carry many group and source records at once, and the RP advertises support with a Packing Capability bit in its Register-Stop messages.
tldr.outcome: Routers can exchange far fewer PIM messages while staying compatible with routers that do not support packing.

today: RFC 9465 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2023, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 7761 and the message type space of RFC 9436.

sections.title: The Problem with One Message per Source
sections.content:
In PIM Sparse Mode (PIM-SM), the Designated Router (DR) periodically sends Null-Register messages to the Rendezvous Point (RP) to keep the state of existing multicast sources alive. Each message describes a single source and group. As the number of sources grows, so does the number of messages, which means more PIM packet processing at both the RP and the DR.

RFC 9465 defines a way to pack the content of multiple Null-Register and Register-Stop messages (from RFC 7761) into a single message. It also covers interoperability with routers that do not support the packed formats.
sections.eli5: Every kid on the bus has to say "I'm still here" to the teacher, one at a time. That takes forever when the bus is full.

sections.title: Advertising the Packing Capability
sections.content:
The RP signals that it can receive PIM Packed Null-Register messages and send PIM Packed Register-Stop messages by setting a Packing Capability bit (P-bit, flag bit 0) in the PIM Register-Stop message. The Register-Stop uses the common header defined in RFC 9436, followed by the Group Address (Encoded-Group format) and Source Address (Encoded-Unicast format) from RFC 7761.

When the feature is enabled, an RP supporting this specification MUST set the P-bit in all Register-Stop messages.
sections.eli5: The teacher puts up a sign saying "I can read group lists now." Only then do the kids switch to the list.

sections.title: The Packed Message Formats
sections.content:
Two message types are defined. The PIM Packed Null-Register is type and subtype 13.0, and the PIM Packed Register-Stop is 13.1. Both start with the PIM common header (version, type, subtype, flag bits and checksum) followed by N records, where each record is a Group Address and Source Address pair.

After the common header, records are parsed one by one until the end of the message, and the length is inferred from the IP layer. Sending or receiving a packed message has the same effect as sending or receiving an individual message for each record in it.
sections.eli5: The packed message is a list. Each line says which group and which sender, and the receiver reads down the list until it runs out of lines.

sections.title: How the DR and RP Switch Over
sections.content:
A DR still sends Register messages when it detects a new source. When it receives a Register-Stop with the P-bit set, it SHOULD send PIM Packed Null-Register messages instead of multiple Register messages with the N-bit set. It MAY mix packed Null-Registers and ordinary Registers, but it is RECOMMENDED to stick to the packed formats while both ends have the feature enabled.

After receiving a Packed Null-Register, the RP SHOULD start sending Packed Register-Stop messages to that DR instead of individual Register-Stops, with the same freedom to mix and the same recommendation.

A DR that learns of packing capability only from the RP's Register-Stop will never use the new format toward an RP that cannot handle it. A DR that does not support packing keeps sending ordinary Null-Registers as defined in Section 4.4 of RFC 7761.
sections.eli5: The kids only switch to the list once the teacher's sign is up. Kids who never learned the list keep calling out one at a time, and that still works.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
In a PIM Anycast RP setup (RFC 4610, and the MSDP variant in RFC 3446), the packed format should be enabled only if every router in the Anycast-RP set supports it.

If an RP stops supporting the feature, for example after a software downgrade, it will not answer a Packed Null-Register with a Register-Stop. When the DR switches to Data Registers from Null-Registers, it MUST start a Packed_Register_Probe_Time timer, default 60 seconds and configurable. If no Packed Register-Stop or Register-Stop with the P-bit arrives in that time, the DR can conclude the RP no longer supports packing, and MAY send an unpacked Null-Register to check the P-bit again. If the network manager disables the capability at the RP, the router MUST NOT advertise it, though it MAY still parse packed registers it receives.

For fragmentation, the DR or RP may perform Path MTU Discovery as described in Section 4.4.1 of RFC 7761, and the number of records per message should be limited so it fits within the Path MTU.
sections.eli5: If the teacher stops reading lists, the kids notice nobody answers after a minute and go back to calling out one by one. Also, do not write a list too long to fit on one page.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7761 apply. The effect of forging a packed message is amplified to all the records in it instead of just one. An attacker who forges a Register-Stop with the P-bit set can trigger a DR to use Packed Null-Registers, creating unnecessary churn in the network.

IANA assigned the Packing Capability bit (0) in the PIM Register-Stop common header, message type 13.0 for Packed Null-Register and 13.1 for Packed Register-Stop in the "PIM Message Types" registry. Flag bits 0-3 of the two new types are "Unassigned".
sections.eli5: A forged list could fool the teacher about many kids at once, so the list makes a trick bigger, not smaller.
